summary: Describes general definitions and mechanisms for establishing Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespaces. A URN namespace gives a family of identifiers their own rules. It is a best current practice that replaces RFC 2611 and was later replaced by RFC 8141.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3406 explains how a group of names becomes an official URN namespace. It describes three kinds of namespace, the form each one's identifier takes, and the paperwork a registrant must complete so that IANA can assign an identifier that will not clash with anyone else's.

questions: how to register a urn namespace

subtitle: How a family of names becomes a registered URN namespace.

tldr.problem: A URN is only useful if it stays assigned to the same resource forever. That cannot be left to chance, so someone has to decide which families of names are allowed to exist and who is in charge of handing them out.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3406 divides URN namespaces into experimental, informal and formal types, and gives a registration process for each. The registrant fills in a template describing the namespace, and IANA or the IESG assigns the namespace identifier that makes the names unique.
tldr.outcome: A formal namespace goes through the full IETF process and is published as an RFC, while an informal one is registered with IANA after a two-week discussion. The document replaced RFC 2611 and was later obsoleted by RFC 8141.

today: RFC 3406 is a Best Current Practice that replaced RFC 2611 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 8141. The RFC points to the IANA registry of URN namespaces for the current list of registered namespaces.

sections.title: Two Managed Spaces
sections.content:
Uniform Resource Names are resource identifiers with the specific requirements for enabling location-independent identification of a resource and longevity of reference. They are part of the larger Uniform Resource Identifier family, with the specific goal of providing persistent naming of resources.

The document rests on two assumptions. The first is that assignment of a URN is a managed process: not all strings that conform to the URN syntax are valid URNs, because a URN is assigned according to the rules of a particular namespace in terms of syntax, semantics and process. The second is that the space of URN namespaces is managed: not all syntactically correct namespaces are valid, because a namespace must have a recognised definition in order to be valid.

The purpose of the document is to outline a mechanism and provide a template for explicit namespace definition, and to provide the mechanism for associating an identifier, called a Namespace ID or NID, which is registered with IANA. The document restricts itself to the processes for creating namespaces. If resolution of any such identifier is wanted, a separate registration in a global NID directory, such as the one provided by the DDDS system, is necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things are managed rather than left open. The names themselves are handed out under rules, and the set of namespaces is itself registered, so that two groups cannot quietly mint the same identifiers.

sections.title: What a URN Namespace Is
sections.content:
For the purposes of URNs, a namespace is a collection of uniquely assigned identifiers. The identifiers are never assigned to more than one resource, and they are never reassigned to a different resource. A single resource may, however, have more than one URN assigned to it for different purposes.

A namespace has an identifier of its own so that URNs are globally unique, and, where desired, so that the identifier gives a cue about the structure of the name that follows it.

The example given is that many identifier systems use strings of numbers, such as ISBN, ISSN and telephone numbers. It is conceivable that the same string could be a valid identifier in two different established systems. Using different designators for the two collections ensures that no two URNs are the same for different resources, because each collection is required to assign each identifier uniquely.

The development of an identifier structure, and with it a collection of identifiers, depends on the requirements of the community defining it, on how the identifiers will be assigned and on the uses they will be put to. Those questions belong to the community, not to the IETF URN work. The document's part is to outline the process by which a collection of identifiers satisfying the constraints can become a bona fide URN namespace by obtaining a NID: in short, a template for the definition of the namespace is completed for deposit with IANA, and a NID is assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN namespace is a family of names where each name is given out exactly once and never reused. The namespace gets a short identifier of its own, so that the same digits under two different namespaces can name two different things.

sections.title: Three Types of Namespace
sections.content:
The document defines three categories of URN namespace, distinguished by the expected level of service and by the procedures required for registration.

Experimental namespaces are not registered with IANA. They take the form X- followed by the NID, and no provision is made to avoid collisions between them, so they are meant for internal or limited experimental use only.

Informal namespaces are fully fledged URN namespaces, with all the rights and requirements that go with them, and can be registered in global registration services. They must uphold the general principles of a well-managed namespace, providing persistent identification of resources and unique assignment of identifier strings. They differ from formal namespaces in how the NID is assigned: IANA assigns an alphanumeric NID to a registered informal namespace.

Formal namespaces are ones where the publication of the NID proposal and of the underlying namespace will benefit some subset of users on the Internet. A formal NID proposal must be functional on and with the global Internet, not limited to users in communities or networks not connected to the Internet. The community that actively uses the names may be small, but the potential use of the names must be open to any user on the Internet.

Formal namespaces may still have aspects that are not fully open, such as a fee-based, privately managed or proprietary registry for assigning URNs, as long as the services associated have openly published access protocols. A formal request must be accompanied by documented considerations of the need for a new namespace and of the community benefit of establishing it formally, and by some consideration of the longevity and maintainability of the namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three levels. An experimental namespace is a name you make up for your own use. An informal namespace is registered with IANA and behaves properly. A formal namespace goes through IETF review and must be open to anyone on the Internet, even if only a few people will actually use it.

sections.title: Registering and Updating a Namespace
sections.content:
The official list of registered URN namespaces is maintained by IANA, and registrations are posted in the IANA registry of URN namespaces. Since URNs are meant to be persistently useful, few changes should be made to the structural interpretation of URN strings, for instance adding or removing rules for lexical equivalence that might affect identifiers already assigned. Clarifications and expansions of the list of authorised assigners may still be important over the life of a namespace.

An experimental namespace needs no registration and therefore no maintenance procedures. An informal namespace is registered with IANA and assigned an identifier in the form urn- followed by a number, chosen by IANA on a first come first served basis. The registrant sends the completed registration template to the urn-nid discussion list and allows a two week discussion period for clarifying the registration information and suggesting technical improvements to the namespace proposal. After the clarifications are incorporated, the template goes to IANA for assignment of the NID. The only restrictions on the number are that it consists strictly of digits and that it does not push the NID past the length limit in the URN syntax.

A formal namespace is assigned by IETF consensus, through an RFC approved by the IESG. The RFC need not be standards track, but it is subject to IESG review. It must include a Namespace Considerations section setting out the perceived need for a new namespace, a Community Considerations section saying how the community will benefit and how a general Internet user could use the space, and an IANA Considerations section indicating that the document carries a registration to be entered in the IANA registry of URN NIDs. The proposed template also goes to the urn-nid list for a two week discussion before the IESG reviews the document.

A particular NID string may be requested for a formal namespace, subject to constraints: it must not already be registered, it must not start with x-, which is reserved for experimental namespaces, it must not start with urn-, which is used for informal namespaces, it must not start with two letters followed by a hyphen, and it must be more than two letters long. All two-letter combinations are reserved for possible country-code based NIDs for eventual national registrations.
sections.plainLanguage: An informal namespace is registered by email, after two weeks of public discussion. A formal namespace has to be written up as an RFC and approved by the IETF's steering group. Either way, IANA ends up holding the list of which namespace identifier belongs to whom.

sections.title: The Namespace Definition Template
sections.content:
A namespace is defined by completing a template. The information is designed to disclose the structure of the namespace and to be useful both to entities seeking a URN assigned in a namespace and to entities seeking to provide URN resolvers for one. That matters for communities evaluating whether to use part of an existing namespace rather than create their own.

The template asks for the namespace identifier, which is assigned by IANA unless a particular string is requested for a formal registration, and for registration information that identifies the version of the registration, starting at 1 and incrementing by one each time, together with the date submitted to IANA in the form YYYY-MM-DD. It asks for the declared registrant, naming the registering organization, its address and a designated contact person with at least one of an email address, a phone number or a postal address.

It then asks for a declaration of the syntactic structure, which may say only that the structure is opaque or may give a regular expression for parsing an identifier into components including naming authorities. It asks for relevant ancillary documentation, such as the RFCs or standards that define the namespace, and for identifier uniqueness considerations, explaining how identifiers are assigned to at most one resource and are never reassigned. It asks about identifier persistence, that is whether the URN stays usable and not merely whether it stays bound to the same resource, and about the process of identifier assignment, which may be completely open, delegated to authorities recognised by an organisation, or completely closed.

Finally it asks about the process for identifier resolution, which matters for namespaces intended for global resolution, since such a namespace must be registered in a Resolution Discovery System. It asks for the rules for lexical equivalence, such as whether a hyphenated and a non-hyphenated grouping of the same identifier are the same, and for any special considerations needed to conform to the URN syntax, which is where legacy systems that use reserved characters get their mapping. It also asks about a validation mechanism, so that users do not guess URNs in the namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: The template is the record everyone can read to understand a namespace: who is in charge, how the identifiers are put together, how they are handed out, how they are resolved, and which rules decide that two identifiers are the same.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document largely focuses on providing mechanisms for declaring public information. Nominally, those declarations should be of relatively low security profile. However, there is always the danger of spoofing and of providing misinformation, and the information in these declarations should be taken as advisory.
sections.plainLanguage: The registrations are public statements. Anyone can write something false in one, so a namespace declaration should be read as advice rather than as a guarantee.

viz.caption: The constraints on a requested formal NID string

items.label: Must not already be registered
items.desc: Each NID identifies exactly one namespace.

items.label: Must not start with x-
items.desc: That prefix is reserved for experimental namespaces.

items.label: Must not start with urn-
items.desc: That prefix is used for informal namespaces.

items.label: Must not start with two letters and a hyphen
items.desc: Two-letter combinations are reserved for possible country-code based NIDs.

items.label: Must be more than two letters long
items.desc: Short identifiers are held back for country-code based registrations.

viz.caption: The parts of the namespace definition template

items.title: Namespace ID
items.text: Assigned by IANA, or requested in the case of a formal registration.

items.title: Registration information
items.text: The version number and the date the registration was submitted.

items.title: Declared registrant
items.text: The registering organization, its address and a named contact.

items.title: Syntactic structure
items.text: How the identifiers are put together, or a statement that they are opaque.

items.title: Identifier uniqueness
items.text: How uniqueness of assignment and non-reassignment are ensured.

items.title: Assignment and resolution
items.text: Who hands out the identifiers and how a URN in the namespace is resolved.

items.title: Lexical equivalence
items.text: Any rules the namespace adds for deciding that two identifiers are the same.
